\subsection{Construction Parameterizations}
\label{app:params}

Table~\ref{tab:ontology} names each construction choice; this section gives the
specific parameterization used for every reported result.

\paragraph{Node entities and labels.}
The node axis changes both the node population and the target, so the three
node types define related but distinct prediction problems rather than three
graphs over one problem.
% code/label_factory.py::_generate_meta_m1
N1 nodes are primary records and take the category of the item they describe.
N2 nodes are secondary entities (reviewers, authors) and take the modal
category over the primary records they participate in. N3 nodes are aggregate
entities and take their own category. Table~\ref{tab:nodestats} reports the
node count, class count and majority-class share for each pair, which is the
context needed to compare scores across node types; McFadden pseudo-$R^2$ is
measured against an intercept-only model and so absorbs part of the differing
class prior, but the raw accuracies in Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap_amazon} do not.

\paragraph{Node text and features.}
% code/generic_data_manager.py::get_node_text, get_embeddings
Node text is embedded with Sentence-BERT \texttt{all-MiniLM-L6-v2} into 384
dimensions. T6a concatenates the primary content with its surrounding context,
T6b uses the primary content alone, and T6e carries no text: its node feature
is an all-zero 384-dimensional vector, so the control is structure-only rather
than text-free but still featured.

\paragraph{Edge rules.}
% code/edge_factory.py
E4a connects nodes sharing an aggregate identifier. E4b and E4c are both built
by co-participation through a shared identifier, dispatched per dataset
(\texttt{\_build\_scalar\_gt} and \texttt{\_build\_participation}); on
\textsc{[datasets]} the two dispatches resolve to the same identifier and
therefore build identical edge sets, and we collapse them to a single rule
before scoring (Appendix~\ref{app:duplicates}). E5a connects node pairs whose
text embeddings have cosine similarity at least $0.75$. E5b connects each node
to the $k=5$ nodes whose degree centrality is closest to its own, where
centrality is computed over the E4b graph.

Two properties of E5b should be stated plainly. First, it is not independent of
the E4 axis, since its input is the E4b graph. Second, degree centrality is
heavily tied in these graphs: on 1{,}000-row subsets the fraction of nodes at
centrality zero ranges from $42.7\%$ (History N1) to $95.7\%$ (Sports N2), with
only ArXiv N2 ($9.0\%$) well separated. Among tied nodes the $k$-nearest
criterion has no signal to act on and selects $k$ arbitrary neighbours, so on
most dataset--node-type pairs E5b supplies uniform connectivity ($\approx 4.9$
edges per node, no isolated nodes, on every dataset we measured) rather than a
structural-similarity signal. The choice $k=5$ replaced an earlier $k=50$ after
an audit; on an ArXiv pilot that change left GNN accuracy unchanged
($p=0.30$) but moved the RAGAS composite from $0.359$ to $0.639$. Results on
the E5b arm should be read with that sensitivity in mind.

\paragraph{Degeneracy guard.}
% code/experiment_runner.py::MAX_EDGES
A variant whose graph exceeds $200{,}000$ undirected edges is recorded as
degenerate and not trained. This is the operational form of pruning constraint
(2) in Section~\ref{sec:ontology}.

\paragraph{Node-classification score.}
% code/trainer.py::compute_pseudo_r2, compute_step1_score
Each variant is scored by a floored McFadden pseudo-$R^2$ on the held-out test
nodes of its subset,
\begin{equation}
S \;=\; \max\!\left(0,\; 1 - \frac{\mathrm{LL}_{\text{model}}}{\mathrm{LL}_{\text{null}}}\right),
\qquad
\mathrm{LL} \;=\; \sum_{i \in \text{test}} \log p(y_i),
\end{equation}
where $p_{\text{model}}$ are softmax probabilities and $p_{\text{null}}$ is the
empirical class frequency within that subset's test mask. The score is not
accuracy: it rewards calibration, and flooring at zero means variants that do
worse than the class prior are not ranked against one another.

\paragraph{GraphRAG pipeline.}
% code/graphrag/evaluate_rag.py, run_phase3b_graphrag_eval.py
Each variant's corpus is indexed with a LlamaIndex \texttt{VectorStoreIndex}
over \texttt{text-embedding-3-small}. A query retrieves the top $3$ passages by
dense similarity; retrieved nodes are then expanded along the variant's own
edges by one hop, and the resulting context is capped at $15$ passages. Because
the cap is fixed, denser variants have more of their expansion discarded, and
because T6a passages are longer than T6b passages the two text fidelities do
not present equal token budgets to the judge.

\paragraph{Question generation and validation.}
% code/graphrag/extend_questions_to_300.py
Questions are generated per dataset in three subtypes of $100$
(\texttt{single\_specific}, \texttt{aggregate\_cross\_paper},
\texttt{edge\_multihop}). Validation is a per-subtype pilot: a sample of each
subtype is scored for RAGAS faithfulness against a flat vector index that is
independent of any graph construction, and a subtype whose pilot falls below
$0.5$ is dropped in full. This is why History retains $233$ questions
($100/100/33$) while the other datasets retain $300$ --- one subtype was
dropped, rather than $67$ individual questions failing. Because the gate runs
against a construction-agnostic index, it does not bias the benchmark toward
any variant. The generator and the judge are both GPT-4o-mini, so the retrieval
scores are not independent of the model that produced the answers.
